title: Akhilleus' sleepless grief
greek: ἄλλοτ' ἐπὶ πλευρὰς κατακείμενος, ἄλλοτε δ' αὖτε ὕπτιος, ἄλλοτε δὲ πρηνής (allot' epi pleuras katakeimenos, allote d' aute hyptios, allote de prēnēs)
short: While the others sleep, Akhilleus tosses on his side, back and face, wanders the shore, and each dawn drags Hector three times round Patroclus' barrow.
body: The book opens with the end of the games and the return of private grief. Akhilleus remembers all he shared with Patroclus, 'the wars of men and the grievous waves'. Leaf notes that a run of five iterative verbs (ending in -sk-) shows this is not one night but a routine repeated over the twelve days before the gods intervene (24.31, 413). Plato quoted these lines in the Republic (3.388a-b) as an example of unworthy lamentation by a hero, unsuitable for the education of guardians. The dragging of Hector 'round the barrow' turns the funeral rite of circling the dead (23.13) into an act of outrage. This picture of restless, unending mourning is what the book will resolve: Akhilleus' grief has to find a limit, as Apollo argues (24.46-9) and as Akhilleus himself will tell Priam (24.549-51).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.12
Plato, Republic 3.388a-b
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.1-21

title: The Judgement of Paris
greek: Ἀλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ' ἄτης (Alexandrou heneka atēs); μαχλοσύνη (machlosynē)
short: The Iliad's only explicit reference to the Judgement of Paris: Paris insulted Hera and Athena and favoured the goddess who offered him lust.
body: Hera, Poseidon and Athena alone oppose returning Hector's body, because of 'the atē (blind folly) of Alexander', who 'reproached' the goddesses when they came to his sheepfold and 'praised her who gave him grievous lust (machlosynē)'. This is the beauty contest decided by Paris, in which Aphrodite won by offering Helen; the Cypria told it at length (Proclus' summary). Aristarchus rejected lines 25-30 (perhaps also 24), partly because Homer nowhere else mentions the Judgement, and partly because machlosynē was thought a word for female wantonness; Leaf finds the objections to lines 29-30 'absolutely convincing' and thinks the whole scheme of Hermes stealing the body may be a later addition. Karl Reinhardt and many later scholars argued the passage is genuine and that the Judgement underlies the hostility of Hera and Athena to Troy throughout the poem (for example 4.31-67, 20.313-17).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIV, p. 535, and notes on 24.23-30
Karl Reinhardt, Das Parisurteil (Frankfurt, 1938)

N. J. Richardson, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 6: Books 21-24 (Cambridge, 1993), notes on 24.25-30

title: Apollo's indictment: Akhilleus as a lion; 'senseless clay'
greek: λέων δ' ὣς ἄγρια οἶδεν (leōn d' hōs agria oiden); κωφὴν γαῖαν (kōphēn gaian)
short: Apollo tells the gods Akhilleus has lost pity and behaves like a lion that obeys only its strength; he outrages 'senseless earth'.
body: Apollo's speech is the moral turning point of the book. Akhilleus' mind is not 'bendable'; he 'knows savage things like a lion', who 'yielding to his great might and proud spirit' attacks men's flocks to get a meal. The lion is the standard Homeric image of the fighting hero, but here it is an image of something less than human: appetite without restraint. Leaf notes the unusual grammar of the simile and the ancient debate over whether Homer used 'feast' (dais) of animals. Apollo ends: Akhilleus is 'outraging dumb earth' (kōphē gaia), for the dead body can feel nothing. Leaf compares Sophocles (Electra 244-5) and Euripides (fragment 537 Nauck) on the dead as mere earth and shadow. The image returns at 24.572, when Akhilleus leaps out of the hut 'like a lion' after his flash of anger at Priam.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.41-3 and 24.54
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.39-54

anchor: neither is shame in his heart
title: Aidōs: shame, respect, restraint
greek: οὐδέ οἱ αἰδώς γίγνεται (oude hoi aidōs gignetai)
short: Apollo says Akhilleus has lost pity and aidōs, the sense of shame and respect that restrains a person; Priam will appeal to exactly that feeling.
body: Aidōs is one of the central Homeric ethical words: the inhibition felt before the gods, before others' judgement, before suppliants, elders or the dead. It keeps warriors in line (5.787) and makes a host protect a guest. Apollo pairs it with eleos, pity: Akhilleus has lost both. Line 24.45, which says aidōs 'harms men greatly and also helps them', is identical with Hesiod, Works and Days 318; Aristarchus athetized it as borrowed from Hesiod, and Leaf agreed that it is senseless here, noting the commonplace of 'two kinds' of aidōs (Euripides, Hippolytus 385-6). Douglas Cairns' study of the concept treats this passage and Priam's later plea, 'have aidōs for the gods, Achilles, and pity me' (aideio theous ... eleēson, 24.503), as a matched pair: the book shows the two feelings returning.

sources.cite: Douglas L. Cairns, Aidōs: The Psychology and Ethics of Honour and Shame in Ancient Greek Literature (Oxford, 1993)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.44-5
Hesiod, Works and Days 317-19
LSJ s.v. αἰδώς

anchor: an enduring soul have the Fates
title: The Moirai (Fates) and the 'enduring heart'
greek: τλητὸν γὰρ Μοῖραι θυμὸν θέσαν ἀνθρώποισιν (tlēton gar Moirai thymon thesan anthrōpoisin)
short: Others lose a brother or a son, weep, and stop, 'for the Fates have given men an enduring heart'; the only plural Moirai in the Iliad.
body: Apollo argues that grief has a natural limit: people lose those dearer than a friend, mourn, and let go. Moira normally means a person's 'portion' or allotted fate, usually singular and only half personified (as at 24.209). Leaf notes that the plural Moirai here, found nowhere else in the Iliad, implies the distinct personified Fates familiar from Hesiod's Theogony (Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, 218, 905), and he counts it among the signs of the book's lateness. Tlētos is also unusual: here active, 'able to endure'. The thought anticipates Akhilleus' own philosophy of suffering in his speech to Priam, in which mortals must bear what the gods spin for them (24.522-51). The verb tlēnai, 'to endure', recurs at the climax, when Priam says he has 'endured' what no mortal ever has (24.505).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.49
Hesiod, Theogony 217-22, 904-6
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.49

anchor: nowise failed he of acceptable gifts
title: Hector's sacrifices and the gods' reciprocity
greek: οὐ γάρ μοί ποτε βωμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης, λοιβῆς τε κνίσης τε (ou gar moi pote bōmos edeueto daitos eïsēs, loibēs te knisēs te)
short: Zeus says Hector was dearest to the gods of all in Troy, because his altar never lacked feast, libation and the savour of burnt fat.
body: Homeric religion is openly reciprocal: men give the gods sacrifice, the gods' 'privilege' (geras, 24.70, the same word used of the dead's due at 23.9), and expect favour in return. Apollo has already reproached the gods for forgetting Hector's 'thighs of bulls and goats' (24.33-4). Zeus' reply repeats the lines he spoke about Troy itself in Book IV (4.48-9): the altar never lacked the 'equal feast', the drink-offering and the knisē, the savour of fat rising in smoke. The divine protection of Hector's body is presented as payment for that piety. Priam draws the same conclusion when Hermes tells him the body is unharmed: 'it is good to give the immortals their due gifts', since Hector never forgot them (24.425-8). Zeus also insists the honour of Achilles and Hector 'shall not be the same', balancing Hera's protest.

sources.cite: C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.66-70
LSJ s.v. κνίσα (κνίση)

title: Simile: Iris dives like a lead weight on a fishing line
greek: μολυβδαίνῃ ἰκέλη ... κατ' ἀγραύλοιο βοὸς κέρας ἐμβεβαυῖα (molybdainēi ikelē ... kat' agrauloio boos keras embebauia)
short: Iris leaps into the sea between Samos (Samothrace) and Imbros and sinks like a lead weight set in an ox-horn, carrying death to the fish.
body: Iris goes to summon Thetis from her sea-cave, diving into the water between 'Samos' (here Samothrace, as at 13.12) and rocky Imbros, islands of the northern Aegean near Troy. The simile is technical. The ancient explanation, reported by Leaf from Aristarchus and Plutarch, was that a small tube of horn was slipped over the line above the hook to stop fish biting through, with lead to sink it. Leaf preferred a newer suggestion (Haskins) that the 'horn' was a lure of polished horn weighted with lead and drawn through the water, like those used in the Pacific. Plato's Ion (538d) quotes these lines when Socrates argues that a fisherman, not a rhapsode, is the right judge of them. The deadly lure falling on the fish is an ominous image for a messenger whose news leads to Akhilleus' surrender of Hector.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.78 and 24.80
Plato, Ion 538d

title: Ransom (apoina): the poem's ring composition
greek: νεκροῖο δὲ δέξαι ἄποινα (nekroio de dexai apoina)
short: Thetis tells Akhilleus to release Hector and accept ransom: the Iliad, which began with a father's rejected ransom, ends with a father's accepted one.
body: Apoina is compensation paid to recover a captive or a body, or to settle a wrong. The Iliad opens with Chryses, an old priest, bringing 'boundless ransom' (apereisia apoina, 1.13) for his daughter and being driven away by Agamemnon, which sets off the plague and the quarrel. It closes with another old father, Priam, bringing 'boundless ransom' (24.276, 502) for his son, and this time it is accepted. Ancient editors gave Book XXIV the title Hektoros lytra, 'the ransoming of Hector'. Cedric Whitman's analysis of the poem's large-scale ring composition, and Colin Macleod's commentary, treat the correspondence of Books I and XXIV as fundamental to its design. Priam's gifts are listed with care (24.228-37): robes, cloaks, coverlets, ten talents of gold, tripods, cauldrons and a precious Thracian cup. Akhilleus had once refused Agamemnon's gifts (Book IX); now he accepts Priam's.

sources.cite: Cedric H. Whitman, Homer and the Heroic Tradition (Cambridge, MA, 1958)
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), Introduction
LSJ s.v. ἄποινα

anchor: Of iron verily is thy heart
title: 'Your heart is iron'
greek: σιδήρειόν νύ τοι ἦτορ (sidēreion ny toi ētor)
short: Hecuba tells Priam his heart must be iron to face Akhilleus; Akhilleus uses the same words to Priam when he arrives.
body: Iron in Homer stands for what is hard, unyielding and unfeeling. Hector used the image of Akhilleus himself as he died: 'the heart in you is iron' (22.357). Hecuba now applies it to Priam, meaning a reckless courage that ignores danger; when Priam actually reaches the hut, Akhilleus greets him with the identical half-line, 'iron is your heart' (24.521), in wonder that he dared to come alone. The repetition is typical of the book's design, in which words spoken in Troy are echoed in Akhilleus' hut. It also shifts the meaning of the metaphor: the iron that meant Akhilleus' cruelty in Book XXII now names the endurance of a grieving father, admired by his son's killer. Compare Odysseus' 'iron' heart and limbs in the Odyssey (Od. 12.280).

sources.cite: C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.205 and 24.521
LSJ s.v. σιδήρεος

title: Fate as spinner
greek: Μοῖρα κραταιὴ γιγνομένῳ ἐπένησε λίνῳ (Moira krataiē gignomenōi epenēse linōi)
short: Hecuba says mighty Moira spun Hector's fate with her thread on the day she bore him: to feed dogs far from his parents.
body: The image of fate spun at birth appears in a few late passages of Homer: Aisa spun Akhilleus' lot with her thread (20.127-8), and in the Odyssey the 'Spinners' (Klōthes) spin for each man at birth (Od. 7.196-8). It becomes the three Moirai, Clotho ('Spinner') among them, in Hesiod. The metaphor joins two women's activities, childbirth and spinning, so that Hecuba speaks as a mother of what was 'spun' while she herself gave birth. It returns at the centre of Akhilleus' great speech: 'this is how the gods have spun (epeklōsanto) for wretched mortals, to live in pain' (24.525). Leaf notes the debate over whether hōs here means 'thus' or 'as'. The motif binds the Trojan mother and the Greek hero in a single view of human life.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.209-10
Homer, Iliad 20.127-8; 24.525; Odyssey 7.196-8
LSJ s.v. ἐπινέω (to spin)

anchor: fix my teeth and feed thereon
title: Hecuba's wish to eat Akhilleus' liver
greek: τοῦ ἐγὼ μέσον ἧπαρ ἔχοιμι ἐσθέμεναι προσφῦσα (tou egō meson hēpar echoimi esthemenai prosphysa)
short: Hecuba wishes she could sink her teeth into Akhilleus' liver and eat it: the poem's last expression of hatred so extreme it becomes cannibal.
body: The wish belongs to a chain of such images. Zeus tells Hera she would eat Priam and his children raw to satisfy her anger (4.34-6), and Akhilleus tells the dying Hector he wishes his fury would drive him to carve and eat his flesh raw (22.346-7). Hecuba's words answer Akhilleus' in kind: then there would be 'requital' (antita erga) for her son. Leaf compares Beatrice in Much Ado About Nothing ('I would eat his heart in the market-place') and warns against reading such curses as evidence of real cannibalism in early Greece. The image marks the limit to which grief and hate drive human beings in the poem; the meal Akhilleus and Priam actually share later in this book (24.621-8) is the opposite, a return to ordinary human eating.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.213
Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (Leiden, 1971)

title: Mestor, son of Priam (not Nestor)
greek: Μήστορά τ' ἀντίθεον (Mēstora t' antitheon)
short: The Greek here names Mestor, one of Priam's dead sons; 'Nestor', the old king of Pylos, is a slip in this text.
body: In his bitter speech to his surviving sons Priam lists the best of those he has lost: 'godlike Mestor, Troilus the chariot-fighter, and Hector, who was a god among men'. The Greek has Mēstora, accusative of Mēstōr, and 'Nestor' in this text is an error, probably a misprint or a slip in transcription, since Nestor of Pylos is an Achaean and alive. Leaf notes that Mestor 'appears only here' in Homer; nothing else is known of him. The name, from mēdomai ('to plan, devise'), means something like 'counsellor'. The error is worth noticing because the name Nestor is so familiar from the games of Book XXIII that a reader might easily take the line to refer to him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.257
Homer, Iliad 24.253-62 (Greek text ed. Murray, Loeb, 1924)
LSJ s.v. μήστωρ

title: Troilus
greek: Τρωΐλον ἱππιοχάρμην (Trōïlon hippiocharmēn)
short: Troilus, a young son of Priam killed by Akhilleus, is mentioned only here in Homer; later he became the hero of the medieval love story of Troilus and Criseyde.
body: Hippiocharmēs means one who fights from a chariot. Homer gives only the name, but the Cypria, according to Proclus' summary, told how Akhilleus killed Troilus, and early vase-painters (most famously on the François Vase, c. 570 BC) showed Akhilleus ambushing Troilus and his sister Polyxena at a fountain outside Troy; a late tradition held that Troy could not fall if Troilus reached the age of twenty. Virgil shows him dragged by his own horses (Aeneid 1.474-8). His later fame is entirely post-classical: Benoît de Sainte-Maure's Roman de Troie (twelfth century) gave him a love affair, developed by Boccaccio (Filostrato), Chaucer (Troilus and Criseyde) and Shakespeare (Troilus and Cressida). In the Iliad he is one more name in Priam's list of the dead, a reminder of how much of the Trojan story lies outside the poem.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.257
Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth (Baltimore, 1993), on Troilus
Proclus, Chrestomathy, summary of the Cypria, in M. L. West, Greek Epic Fragments (Loeb, 2003)
Virgil, Aeneid 1.474-8

title: The eagle omen on the right
greek: αἰετὸν ... μόρφνον θηρητῆρ' ὃν καὶ περκνὸν καλέουσιν (aieton ... morphnon thērētēr' hon kai perknon kaleousin)
short: Priam pours a libation and asks Zeus for a bird sign; Zeus sends his eagle on the right, and the Trojans take heart.
body: Hecuba insists on proper ritual: Priam washes his hands, pours wine from a golden cup, and asks Zeus of Ida for 'his swift messenger', the bird dearest to him, to appear on the right, the lucky side for a Greek observer. Zeus answers with 'the most perfect of birds', the eagle. Morphnos and perknos, both meaning something like 'dark', occur only here in Homer; Leaf notes that Aristotle (History of Animals 9.32) identifies a kind of eagle called morphnos and adds that Homer mentions it in the account of Priam's journey. The wingspan is compared to the wide double doors of a rich man's treasure-chamber, an image that suits a scene full of treasure. The same pattern of prayer and answering eagle appears elsewhere (8.245-52; Od. 15.160-5), but here it gives a frightened old man the confidence to cross enemy lines.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.316
Aristotle, History of Animals 9.32, 618b
Homer, Iliad 24.283-321

title: Hermes the guide (the 'Helper', Argeiphontes)
greek: εἵλετο δὲ ῥάβδον, τῇ τ' ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει (heileto de rhabdon, tēi t' andrōn ommata thelgei); ἐριούνιος (eriounios)
short: Zeus sends Hermes, the god who 'loves to be a companion to men', with golden sandals and the wand that charms men to sleep, to escort Priam through the camp.
body: Hermes, not Iris, is the escort, and Leaf counts this among the book's links with the Odyssey: the lines on his sandals and wand recur at Od. 5.44-8, and the description of him as a young prince 'with the first down on his lip' at Od. 10.278-9. His wand (rhabdos) puts men to sleep or wakes them; in Odyssey XXIV he uses it to lead the souls of the dead to Hades. Murray's 'the Helper' renders eriounios, an old epithet of uncertain origin. Hermes meets Priam at dusk by the tomb of Ilus, invents a cover story (a Myrmidon squire, son of 'Polyctor', 24.396-400) worthy of Odysseus, puts the guards to sleep and opens Akhilleus' gate. Douglas Frame and others have read Priam's night journey, led by the escort of the dead, as a symbolic descent to the underworld and return.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIV, p. 536, and notes on 24.347 and 24.360
Douglas Frame, The Myth of Return in Early Greek Epic (New Haven, 1978), Epilogue
LSJ s.v. ἐριούνιος

title: Hector's body 'dewy-fresh'
greek: οἷον ἐερσήεις κεῖται (hoion eersēeis keitai)
short: Hermes tells Priam that after twelve days Hector lies 'dewy-fresh', washed of blood, his wounds closed: the gods have kept him whole.
body: Eersēeis, 'dewy', means fresh as if newly dead. Leaf explains that the body has not been parched by the sun because Apollo spread a cloud over it (23.188-91); Apollo has also covered it with the golden aegis while it was dragged (24.18-21), the god's protective shield. Hermes adds that worms and decay have not touched it and that the many wounds made by Achaean spears are closed. Hecuba uses the same word in her lament, comparing Hector to a man killed suddenly by Apollo's 'gentle arrows' (24.757-9). The miracle has a double meaning: Akhilleus' attempt to outrage the corpse has failed, and the body can now be returned and mourned as if death had only just occurred, wiping out the time of outrage. Priam reads it as the gods' reward for Hector's sacrifices.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.419
Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (Leiden, 1971)

title: Akhilleus' hut and its great bolt
greek: θύρην δ' ἔχε μοῦνος ἐπιβλὴς εἰλάτινος (thyrēn d' eche mounos epiblēs eilatinos)
short: The Myrmidons have built their king a hall with a courtyard and a door bar of fir that took three men to move, though Akhilleus could work it alone.
body: Leaf observes that the 'hut' (klisiē) is here described as a full Homeric house, with fenced courtyard, porch, portico and hall, a picture he found consistent elsewhere only with Book IX. The bar (epiblēs) is a long beam slid across the door into holes in the posts. That three ordinary Achaeans were needed to shoot it home and three to draw it back, but Akhilleus could do it alone, recalls the Pelian ash spear that only Akhilleus could wield (16.140-4). The detail prepares a key moment: Hermes opens it for Priam, and later Akhilleus, angry and suspicious, tells Priam he knows a god must have brought him, since no mortal could have passed the guards 'or easily pushed back the bar of our doors' (24.565-7). The house at the edge of the sea becomes the setting of the poem's last great scene.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIV, p. 536, and notes on 24.448 and 24.453

title: Supplication: Priam kisses the man-slaying hands
greek: λάβε γούνατα καὶ κύσε χεῖρας δεινὰς ἀνδροφόνους (labe gounata kai kyse cheiras deinas androphonous)
short: Priam clasps Akhilleus' knees and kisses 'the terrible, man-slaying hands that had killed his many sons': the climactic act of supplication in the poem.
body: Supplication (hikesia) was a formal ritual: the suppliant crouched, clasped the knees of the person entreated and touched the chin or hands; once accepted, he was under the protection of Zeus Hikesios. John Gould's classic study analysed these gestures. Supplication on the battlefield has failed throughout the Iliad: Akhilleus killed Lycaon as he held his knees (21.64-119). Here the gesture is extreme because of the hands Priam kisses: androphonous, 'man-slaying', the epithet earlier used of Akhilleus' hands as he laid them on Patroclus' breast (18.317, 23.18) and regularly of Hector himself. Priam enters 'unseen', as Zeus planned, and is suddenly physically present. Kevin Crotty reads the scene as the poem's model of how supplication can produce pity and mutual recognition rather than further violence.

sources.cite: John Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973) 74-103
Kevin Crotty, The Poetics of Supplication: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey (Ithaca, 1994)

title: Simile: Priam as a homicide seeking refuge
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἂν ἄνδρ' ἄτη πυκινὴ λάβῃ (hōs d' hot' an andr' atē pykinē labēi)
short: Akhilleus stares at Priam as people stare at a man who has killed someone at home and arrives, an exile, at a rich man's door: a startling reversal of roles.
body: The comparison draws on a familiar situation: the killer who must flee his own land and seek protection from a wealthy chief, as Patroclus did at Peleus' house (23.85-90). Leaf explains atē here as the blind force that drove the man to the killing. The surprise is the reversal: the real killer in the scene is Akhilleus, slayer of Priam's sons, yet it is Priam who is pictured as the homicide begging for shelter, and Akhilleus who plays the rich man who receives him. Wonder (thambos) seizes Akhilleus and his companions, and the word is repeated three times. Leaf notes that the scholia assumed the exile came for ritual purification, but argues there is no trace of purification in Homer, only payment or exile. Macleod and others see the simile as one of the most deliberate inversions in the poem, expressing the strangeness of the meeting.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.480 and 24.482
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.480-4

title: Priam's plea: 'Remember your father'
greek: μνῆσαι πατρὸς σοῖο (mnēsai patros soio); ἀνδρὸς παιδοφόνοιο ποτὶ στόμα χεῖρ' ὀρέγεσθαι (andros paidophonoio poti stoma cheir' oregesthai)
short: Priam asks Akhilleus to remember Peleus, old like himself, and says he has done what no mortal ever did: reached to the face of his sons' killer.
body: Priam's speech is built on one idea: Akhilleus' father Peleus is old, perhaps harassed by neighbours, but still hopes to see his son return; Priam has lost fifty sons, the best of them Hector. He begs Akhilleus to have aidōs for the gods and pity for him (24.503). The final line (24.506) is debated. Leaf takes it as 'to reach my hand to the mouth (chin) of the man who killed my children', the suppliant's gesture of touching the chin (compare Thetis, 1.500-1); others read it as 'to bring to my mouth the hand of the child-slayer', that is, to kiss it, which matches the kiss just described. Murray's 'reach forth my hand to the face' follows the first view. Either way the climax is physical contact with the killer. The appeal to Peleus works because it lets Akhilleus see Priam as his own father.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.486 and 24.506
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.486-506

title: Akhilleus and Priam weep together
greek: τὼ δὲ μνησαμένω (tō de mnēsamenō); αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς κλαῖεν ἑὸν πατέρ', ἄλλοτε δ' αὖτε Πάτροκλον (autar Achilleus klaien heon pater', allote d' aute Patroklon)
short: The two enemies remember and weep, Priam for Hector, Akhilleus for his father and for Patroclus: grief becomes the bond between them.
body: The Greek dual (tō ... mnēsamenō, 'the two of them, remembering') binds the men grammatically while their thoughts go to different people. Priam weeps for 'man-slaying Hector' crouched at Akhilleus' feet; Akhilleus weeps for Peleus, whom he will never see again, 'and now again for Patroclus'. Their moaning fills the house. This is the emotional turning point of the poem: the wrath that began over a prize and turned into revenge for Patroclus ends in lament shared with the enemy. Macleod's commentary and much modern criticism treat the scene as the poem's fullest statement of shared human suffering. After the weeping comes reflection: Akhilleus raises Priam, pities his white hair and beard, and begins the speech of the two jars, in which he sets both their sorrows within the common lot of mortals.

sources.cite: C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), Introduction and commentary on 24.507-12
Homer, Iliad 24.507-17
Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death (Oxford, 1980)

title: The two jars of Zeus
greek: δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς οὔδει (doioi gar te pithoi katakeiatai en Dios oudei)
short: Akhilleus tells Priam that Zeus keeps two jars of gifts, one of evils and one of blessings; some men get a mixture, some only evil, none only good.
body: The pithoi are great storage jars, like those in which a household kept grain and wine. Zeus gives mortals a mixture of good and evil, or evil alone; the gods themselves live 'without sorrow'. Leaf records two ancient readings: two jars, one of evils and one of goods, or two jars of evils and a third of goods (Greek eteros can count the first two as a unit). Pindar seems to follow the second: 'for one good, the gods give mortals two evils' (Pythian 3.81-2). Leaf compares the jar opened by Pandora (Hesiod, Works and Days 94). Plato quotes the lines in the Republic (2.379d) and rejects them, insisting that god is the cause only of good. Akhilleus applies the doctrine to Peleus, blessed but given one short-lived son, and to Priam, once rich in sons and wealth: their two lives illustrate the mixed lot.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.527-8
Plato, Republic 2.379d
Pindar, Pythian 3.81-2
Hesiod, Works and Days 90-105

anchor: Be not thou wroth with me
title: Akhilleus' apology to the dead Patroclus
greek: μή μοι Πάτροκλε σκυδμαινέμεν (mē moi Patrokle skydmainemen)
short: Akhilleus asks Patroclus' shade not to be angry that he has returned Hector for a worthy ransom, and promises him his share of it.
body: Akhilleus has had the body washed and anointed out of Priam's sight, fearing that the sight would provoke an outburst and that he might then kill the old man (24.582-6). Before returning to Priam he speaks to Patroclus, as at the pyre ('even in the house of Hades', 23.19, 179). He justifies himself: the ransom is 'not unseemly', and Patroclus will receive his due share of it. Aristarchus rejected lines 594-5, arguing that Akhilleus gave Hector back because Zeus ordered it, not for gifts. Leaf defended them: Zeus' command itself depends on the ransom (24.119, 137-9), and only the ransom lets Akhilleus feel the return is not dishonourable. How Patroclus would receive his share is not said; Leaf suggests offerings burned or buried with his ashes, comparing Andromache's resolve to burn Hector's clothes (22.508-14).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.593-5
N. J. Richardson, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 6: Books 21-24 (Cambridge, 1993), notes on 24.592-5

title: Niobe: a myth told to persuade
greek: καὶ γάρ τ' ἠΰκομος Νιόβη ἐμνήσατο σίτου (kai gar t' ēukomos Niobē emnēsato sitou)
short: Akhilleus urges Priam to eat: even Niobe, whose twelve children Apollo and Artemis killed, remembered food; now she is a weeping stone on Mount Sipylus.
body: Niobe boasted that she had borne many children while Leto had only two; Apollo and Artemis killed all twelve. The bodies lay unburied nine days, until on the tenth the gods buried them, and Niobe 'remembered food'. Malcolm Willcock argued that Homer invented details of such paradigms to fit the situation, taking this as his model case: the eating Niobe exists to persuade Priam to eat. The nine days her children lay unburied also echo Hector's case. Leaf notes this is Homer's only mention of the myth, later the subject of tragedies by Aeschylus and Sophocles, who gave her seven sons and seven daughters. Aristarchus rejected 614-17, where Niobe is a stone that still 'broods on her sorrows' on Mount Sipylus in Lydia; Leaf defends the lines. Pausanias climbed Sipylus and saw the rock, which from a distance looks like a weeping woman (1.21.3).

sources.cite: M. M. Willcock, 'Mythological Paradeigma in the Iliad', Classical Quarterly n.s. 14 (1964) 141-54
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.602 and 24.614-17
Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.21.3

title: Priam and Akhilleus gaze at each other in wonder
greek: Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος θαύμαζ' Ἀχιλῆα ... αὐτὰρ ὃ Δαρδανίδην Πρίαμον θαύμαζεν Ἀχιλλεύς (Dardanidēs Priamos thaumaz' Achilēa ... autar ho Dardanidēn Priamon thaumazen Achilleus)
short: After the meal, Priam marvels at Akhilleus' size and beauty, 'like the gods', and Akhilleus marvels at Priam's noble face and his words.
body: The two sentences mirror each other, with the same verb (thaumazō, 'to wonder at') and the names placed in reverse order. Each sees in the other something admirable rather than an enemy: Priam sees Akhilleus' godlike stature, Akhilleus sees Priam's appearance and hears his speech. The scene follows directly on the shared meal (24.621-8), a formal type-scene of eating that marks Akhilleus' return to normal life after his refusal of food (19.205-14, 19.303-8). Wonder was the first reaction when Priam entered (thambos, 24.480-4); now it is calm and reciprocal. Macleod's commentary treats the passage as one of the book's central moments of recognition. The mood is fragile: Akhilleus' next words, sending Priam to sleep outside, carry a sharp edge.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 24.621-33
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.628-32
LSJ s.v. θαυμάζω

title: Epikertomeōn: 'mockingly' or 'teasingly'?
greek: τὸν δ' ἐπικερτομέων προσέφη (ton d' epikertomeōn prosephē)
short: Murray's 'mockingly' renders a disputed word: Akhilleus may be bitter about Agamemnon, or gently playful as he explains why Priam must sleep outside.
body: Kertomeō and epikertomeō usually mean to taunt or jeer, as a victor speaks over a dying enemy (16.744). Yet nothing in Akhilleus' words to Priam is a taunt: he tells him to sleep in the portico in case an Achaean counsellor comes by and reports him to Agamemnon, which would delay the return of the body. Leaf suggests the word expresses Akhilleus' bitterness toward Agamemnon, whom he expects to obstruct him; he notes the alternative sense 'bantering', which would make the line a half-playful apology for lodging Priam outside, though he thinks this stretches the word. Many modern readers prefer some form of ironic or grim humour. The ambiguity suits the moment: the truce is real but fragile, and Akhilleus remains dangerous. He then asks how many days Priam needs for the funeral.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.649
LSJ s.v. ἐπικερτομέω
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.649

anchor: nine days' space will we wail
title: The truce for Hector's funeral
greek: ἐννῆμαρ ... τῇ δεκάτῃ ... ἑνδεκάτῃ ... τῇ δὲ δυωδεκάτῃ πολεμίξομεν εἴ περ ἀνάγκη (ennēmar ... tēi dekatēi ... hendekatēi ... tēi de dyōdekatēi polemixomen ei per anankē)
short: Priam asks for nine days of mourning, burial on the tenth, a barrow on the eleventh; 'on the twelfth we will fight, if we must'.
body: The count of days is solemn and exact, and it closes a pattern of numbers that runs through the poem's opening and close: in Book I the plague lasts nine days and the gods are away twelve days (1.53, 1.493); in Book XXIV Hector has lain twelve days and Niobe's children nine (24.31, 24.610). Priam explains why the Trojans need so long: they are shut in the city and wood must be brought from far away on the mountain. Akhilleus grants it and takes Priam's right hand at the wrist, 'lest he fear in his heart', a gesture of pledged faith. The last words of the request, 'if we must', keep the war in view; the poem ends with the funeral, not with peace. Cedric Whitman's study of the poem's ring structure draws on such correspondences of days between the first and last books.

sources.cite: Cedric H. Whitman, Homer and the Heroic Tradition (Cambridge, MA, 1958)
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.664-7

title: Briseis beside Akhilleus
greek: τῷ δὲ Βρισηῒς παρελέξατο καλλιπάρῃος (tōi de Brisēïs parelexato kallipārēos)
short: Akhilleus sleeps with Briseis at his side: the woman whose seizure began the quarrel in Book I is back where she was taken from.
body: Briseis, a captive from Lyrnessus, was Akhilleus' prize (geras); Agamemnon's taking of her (1.318-48) caused the wrath with which the poem begins. She was returned with Agamemnon's gifts in Book XIX, where she lamented Patroclus as the one who had been kind to her (19.282-300). The closing image of Akhilleus sleeping 'in the innermost part of the hut' with her beside him echoes Book IX, where he slept with another captive, Diomede, while Briseis was away (9.663-5). It is a signal of normality restored: the hero who refused food, sleep and sex (as Thetis reproached him, 24.128-31) now eats, sleeps and lies with the woman whose loss began everything. The quiet line is one of the book's many returns to the situation of Book I.

sources.cite: C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics, Cambridge, 1982), commentary on 24.675-6
Casey Dué, Homeric Variations on a Lament by Briseis (Lanham, MD, 2002)

title: Cassandra sees Hector returning
greek: Κασσάνδρη ἰκέλη χρυσῇ Ἀφροδίτῃ (Kassandrē ikelē chrysēi Aphroditēi)
short: From the citadel of Pergamus, Cassandra is the first to see Priam bringing Hector's body home, and calls the city out to meet him.
body: Cassandra is named only twice in the Iliad: as the most beautiful of Priam's daughters, promised to the ally Othryoneus (13.365-9), and here. In the Odyssey Agamemnon's ghost hears her death cry as Clytemnestra kills her (Od. 11.421-3). Leaf notes the scholia's remark that Homer gives no sign of her gift of prophecy, so central in the later epic cycle and in Aeschylus' Agamemnon, though nothing here contradicts it; he suggests that the poet's choice of her as the first to see the body may have encouraged later poets to make her the seer who knows. Her cry, 'Come, Trojans and Trojan women, and see Hector, if ever you rejoiced when he came back alive from battle', turns his last homecoming into a bitter reversal of his returns from war.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.699
Homer, Iliad 13.365-9; Odyssey 11.421-3
Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1035-1330

title: The laments for Hector: thrēnos and goos
greek: παρὰ δ' εἷσαν ἀοιδοὺς θρήνων ἐξάρχους (para d' heisan aoidous thrēnōn exarchous)
short: Professional singers lead the formal dirge (thrēnos); then Andromache, Hecuba and Helen each lead a personal lament (goos), answered by the women.
body: Homer distinguishes two kinds of mourning song. The thrēnos is sung by hired singers (aoidoi), 'leaders of the dirge'; the goos is the personal lament of a kinswoman, to which the other women respond with wailing. Margaret Alexiou's study of Greek lament traces this antiphonal pattern from Homer to modern Greek folk practice. Leaf calls the Greek of lines 720-2 very difficult. Three women lament in turn: Andromache, wife; Hecuba, mother; and Helen, sister-in-law. They are the same three women Hector met in Troy in Book VI, and each speaks from her own position: Andromache of the city's fall and her son, Hecuba of the gods' care for his body, Helen of his kindness to her. Their laments form the poem's last speeches, so that the Iliad ends in the voices of women mourning the dead.

sources.cite: Margaret Alexiou, The Ritual Lament in Greek Tradition (Cambridge, 1974)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIV, p. 536, and note on 24.720

title: Andromache foresees Astyanax's death
greek: ῥίψει χειρὸς ἑλὼν ἀπὸ πύργου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον (rhipsei cheiros helōn apo pyrgou lygron olethron)
short: Andromache imagines her son enslaved, or thrown from the walls by some Achaean whose kinsman Hector killed: the fate later epic and tragedy gave him.
body: Andromache's lament looks beyond the poem to the fall of Troy: the women carried off in the ships, the child either a slave or hurled from the tower 'a woeful death'. That is what later tradition made of Astyanax. Leaf cites lines of the Little Iliad, preserved by Tzetzes, in which Akhilleus' son Neoptolemus takes Andromache to the ships and throws the child from the wall; in the Sack of Ilion (Iliou Persis) Proclus' summary says Odysseus killed him. Euripides' Trojan Women dramatizes the death. The prophecy overturns Hector's own prayer in Book VI that his son would grow to be 'far better than his father' (6.476-81). Andromache's lament ends with a private grief: Hector died without stretching out his hands to her from his bed or speaking a last word she could remember.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.735
M. L. West, Greek Epic Fragments (Loeb, 2003): Little Iliad and Iliou Persis

title: Apollo's 'gentle arrows': sudden painless death
greek: οἷς ἀγανοῖσι βέλεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος κατέπεφνεν (hois aganoisi belessin epoichomenos katepephnen)
short: Hecuba says Hector lies fresh as one killed by Apollo's 'gentle shafts', the Greek way of describing a sudden natural death without suffering.
body: Apollo and Artemis, the archer gods, were believed to cause sudden death, Apollo of men and Artemis of women; when the death was quick and painless their arrows were called 'gentle' (aganos). Leaf notes that the line is a favourite in the Odyssey (3.279-80, of a helmsman; 15.410-11; and Odysseus asks his mother's shade whether Artemis killed her with her gentle arrows, 11.172-3) and does not otherwise occur in the Iliad. The same god whose arrows brought the plague in Book I (1.43-52) is here a giver of easy death. The comparison is consoling and ironic: Hector died violently at Akhilleus' hands and was dragged for twelve days, yet thanks to the gods he lies 'dewy-fresh', as if he had died peacefully at home.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.759
LSJ s.v. ἀγανός

title: Helen's 'twentieth year'
greek: τόδε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστὶν (tode eikoston etos estin)
short: Helen says it is now the twentieth year since she left home, though the war has lasted only ten: a puzzle ancient and modern readers have tried to solve.
body: Helen, who has been blamed by everyone in Troy, says Hector never spoke a harsh word to her and restrained others who did. Her statement that twenty years have passed since she left Sparta clashes with the ten-year war of the rest of the poem (2.134, 2.295-6). Leaf sets out the two main explanations. The later epic tradition (the Cypria, reported by Proclus) told of a first, failed expedition that landed by mistake in Mysia, and later writers made the gathering of the second fleet take years more; or the phrase is a mechanical echo of the Odyssey, where the same two lines are used of Odysseus' twenty-year absence (Od. 19.222-3). Leaf took it as a sign of the late composition of the laments; others read it simply as Helen's sense of how long her exile has lasted.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIV, p. 536, and note on 24.765
Homer, Odyssey 19.222-3

title: Hector's funeral
greek: καὶ τά γε χρυσείην ἐς λάρνακα θῆκαν (kai ta ge chryseiēn es larnaka thēkan)
short: Nine days gathering wood, burning on the tenth, the bones placed in a golden chest, a grave, a mound and a feast: Hector receives the full rites.
body: The funeral repeats, in a few lines and the same formulas, the stages of Patroclus' burial in Book XXIII: the pyre quenched with wine, the white bones gathered by brothers and comrades, the remains placed in a golden container (here a larnax, a box or chest), wrapped in soft purple robes, laid in a hollow grave under close-set stones, and covered by a mound, with a funeral feast in Priam's house. Leaf notes later archaeological parallels for the wrapping of ashes in cloth. The contrast with Patroclus' funeral is as telling as the likeness: there are no horses, dogs or captives, and watchers are posted 'lest the Achaeans attack before the time'. The war goes on around the grave. What Akhilleus denied Hector in Book XXII, the 'due of the dead', is finally paid.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 24.795-6
N. J. Richardson, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 6: Books 21-24 (Cambridge, 1993), notes on 24.777-804

title: The last line: 'Hector, tamer of horses'
greek: ὣς οἵ γ' ἀμφίεπον τάφον Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο (hōs hoi g' amphiepon taphon Hektoros hippodamoio)
short: The Iliad ends with Hector's funeral and his traditional epithet 'horse-taming'; an ancient variant joined it to the next epic of the cycle.
body: The poem that began with 'the wrath of Achilles' ends with the burial of his enemy, named with a formulaic epithet, hippodamos, 'tamer of horses', used of Trojans in general and of Hector in particular. Nothing is said of Akhilleus' death or the fall of Troy, though both have been foretold. Leaf records a variant ending in the scholia (Schol. T): 'so they held the funeral of Hector; and there came an Amazon, daughter of great-hearted Ares the man-slayer'. It was evidently made to link the Iliad to the Aethiopis, the next poem of the epic cycle, which told of the Amazon Penthesilea, Memnon and the death of Akhilleus; Quintus of Smyrna's continuation also begins with Penthesilea. The standard ending, closing on a funeral rather than a battle, has been admired since antiquity for its restraint.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 24.804
Proclus, Chrestomathy, summary of the Aethiopis, in M. L. West, Greek Epic Fragments (Loeb, 2003)
